# AMOUNTS {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(theme_ggp2g(
    base_size = 15))
bare_theme <- theme(plot.title = element_blank(),
                    plot.subtitle = element_blank(),
                    plot.caption = element_blank(),
                    axis.title = element_blank(),
                    axis.text = element_blank(),
                    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
                    strip.text = element_blank(),
                    strip.background = element_blank(),
                    legend.position = "none")
```

The graphs in this part show how many there are of something, or a few simple numbers that stand for one or two columns.[^amounts-def]

## Grouped bar graphs

A grouped bar graph compares more than one set of numbers across the same groups.[^grp-vars] Each group gets a few bars that stand side by side, one for each part of the data. The names of the groups run along the foot of the graph, and the values we found run up the side.[^grp-axes] A color for each part shows which bar is which, and a key on the side or top of the graph names the colors.[^grp-legend]

```{r}
#| label: part_grp_bar_graphs
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
jp_dinos <- tibble(
  species = c("Brachiosaurus", "Triceratops", "Tyrannosaurus",
              "Gallimimus", "Velociraptor"),
  n = c(3, 5, 2, 20, 8),
  mean_tons = c(40, 9, 8, 0.45, 0.15),
  sd_tons = c(5, 1.2, 1, 0.08, 0.03)) |>
  tidyr::uncount(n) |>
  mutate(weight_tons = round(rnorm(n(), mean = mean_tons, sd = sd_tons), 2)) |>
  select(species, weight_tons)
jp_paddocks <- jp_dinos |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(total_tons = sum(weight_tons)) |>
  ungroup()
labs_grp_col <- labs(
    title = "Jurassic Park",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    subtitle = "Total weight of the dinosaurs in each paddock",
    x = "Paddock",
    y = "Total weight (tons)")
ggp2_grp_col <- ggplot(data = jp_paddocks,
              aes(x = species, 
                  y = total_tons)) + 
        geom_col(aes(fill = species),
            show.legend = FALSE) +
        scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))
(
  ggp2_grp_col +
      labs_grp_col
) +
  fmggp2::theme_jurassic(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Summary bar graphs

This kind of bar graph shows one number for each group.[^statistic] Each bar stands for a number we worked out from the data in one group, such as the mean, the middle number, or the total.[^median] The names of the groups run along the foot of the graph, and the numbers run up the side. These graphs quickly show the most important numbers for each group, and they can add small lines to show how much the numbers change or how sure we can be about them.[^error-bars]

```{r}
#| label: part_sum_bar_graphs
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
happy_meals <- tibble(
  promotion = c("Teenie Beanie Babies", "Furby", 
                "Hot Wheels", "Inspector Gadget"),
  lambda = c(420, 310, 220, 180)) |>
  tidyr::uncount(28, .id = "day") |>
  mutate(promotion = factor(promotion, levels = unique(promotion)),
         sold = rpois(n(), lambda = lambda)) |>
  select(promotion, day, sold)
hm_sum_col <- happy_meals |> 
  group_by(promotion) |> 
  summarise(avg_sold = mean(sold)) |> 
  ungroup()
labs_sum_col <- labs(
    title = "Happy Meals",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    subtitle = "Average Happy Meals sold per day\nduring each toy promotion",
    x = "Toy promotion",
    y = "Average sold per day")
ggp2_sum_col <- ggplot(data = hm_sum_col,
    aes(x = promotion,
        y = avg_sold)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = promotion), 
        show.legend = FALSE)  
(
  ggp2_sum_col +
      labs_sum_col
) +
  fmggp2::theme_happymeal(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Overlapping bar graphs

When we show more than one set of numbers in one graph, we can put the bars over each other instead of side by side.[^overlap] This way we can compare the groups on the same number line, but the graph can be hard to read if we can't see through the bars. We often make the bars so we can see through them a little, which shows the bars behind them.[^alpha] A key can help tell us which data each bar stands for.

```{r}
#| label: part_overlapping_bar_graphs
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1990)
netware_offices <- tibble(
  year = c("1990", "1994", "1998"),
  mean_nodes = c(22, 24, 27)) |>
  tidyr::uncount(24, .id = "office") |>
  mutate(nodes = round(rnorm(n(), mean = mean_nodes, sd = 2.5)),
         lan_size = if_else(nodes >= 25, "25 or more", "Under 25")) |>
  select(year, office, nodes, lan_size)
labs_bar_ovrlp <- labs(
  title = "Novell NetWare",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Workstations per office LAN in three years",
  x = "Workstations",
  y = "Offices",
  fill = "Year")
ggp2_bar_ovrlp <- ggplot(data = netware_offices,
          aes(x = nodes, fill = year)) +
                geom_bar() 
(
  ggp2_bar_ovrlp +
    labs_bar_ovrlp
) +
  fmggp2::theme_netware(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Heatmaps

A heatmap shows numbers as colors. It uses a table of boxes, with groups along the foot and up the side.[^matrix] Each box gets a color from the number it holds. A heatmap helps show how big something is across two sets of groups. A color key next to the graph often tells us what the colors mean.[^color-scale]

```{r}
#| label: part_heatmaps
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1990)
fp_gags <- tibble(
  gag = c("Will flirts", "Phil yells at Will", "Geoffrey zinger",
          "Jazz thrown out", "Hilary goes shopping", "Carlton dance"),
  base = c(1.5, 1.2, 0.8, -0.4, -0.2, -2.2),
  trend = c(-0.3, -0.1, 0, 0.2, 0, 0.5))
fp_episodes <- fp_gags |>
  tidyr::expand_grid(season = 1:6, episode = 1:24) |>
  mutate(p = plogis(base + trend * (season - 3.5)),
         present = rbinom(n(), size = 1, prob = p))
fp_heatmap <- fp_episodes |>
  group_by(season, gag) |>
  summarise(occurrences = sum(present), .groups = "drop")
labs_heatmap_tile <- labs(
  title = "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Running gags per season (24 episodes each)",
  x = "Season", 
  y = "Running gag", 
  fill = "Episodes")
ggp2_heatmap_tile <- ggplot(data = fp_heatmap, 
       aes(x = season, 
           y = gag, 
           fill = occurrences)) + 
       geom_tile() + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
(
  ggp2_heatmap_tile +
    labs_heatmap_tile
) +
  fmggp2::theme_freshprince(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Waffle charts

A waffle chart is made of small boxes and shows how a whole thing breaks into parts. It does the same job as a round graph cut into pieces, but it gives each part its own small boxes or little pictures and puts them in groups that make one big box.[^grid] This kind of graph works well for showing a part out of a total, like how many out of 100.[^percent] To make it easy to understand, you can add a key or words next to each group to say what it is.

```{r}
#| label: part_waffle_charts
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-asp: 1
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggwaffle)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
pog_collection <- tibble(
  pog_id = 1:100,
  type = sample(c("Milk caps", "Printed pogs", "Holographic", "Slammers"),
    size = 100, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.45, 0.30, 0.15, 0.10)))
waffle_pogs <- ggwaffle::waffle_iron(pog_collection,
                      aes_d(group = type), rows = 10)
labs_waffle <- labs(
  title = "A Pogs collection",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "100 pieces, one square each",
  x = "", y = "", fill = NULL)
ggp2_waffle <- ggplot(data = waffle_pogs, 
       aes(x = x, 
           y = y, 
           fill = group)) + 
  ggwaffle::geom_waffle() +
  coord_equal()
(
  ggp2_waffle +
    labs_waffle +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "top") +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
) +
  fmggp2::theme_pogs(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

## Cleveland dot plots

A Cleveland dot plot shows each number as a point along a line. It helps compare a few different numbers. The graph lists the groups up the side and shows the data as points along a line. It shows the differences between groups, and it does the same work as a bar graph with less on the page.[^efficient]

```{r}
#| label: part_cleveland_dot_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
set.seed(1979)
walkman_tests <- faux::sim_design(
  between = list(model = c("WM2", "Sports", "MegaBass"),
                 battery = c("Alkaline", "Rechargeable")),
  n = 20,
  mu = c(WM2_Alkaline = 10, WM2_Rechargeable = 7,
         Sports_Alkaline = 16, Sports_Rechargeable = 12,
         MegaBass_Alkaline = 22, MegaBass_Rechargeable = 17),
  sd = 2, dv = "hours", long = TRUE, plot = FALSE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("WM2", "Sports", "MegaBass"),
    labels = c("WM-2", "WM-F45 Sports", "WM-EX194 Mega Bass")))
walkman_clev_dots <- walkman_tests |>
  group_by(battery, model) |>
  summarise(med_hours = median(hours), .groups = "drop")
labs_clev_dots <- labs(
    title = "Sony Walkman battery tests",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    subtitle = "Alkaline and rechargeable batteries",
    x = "Median battery life (hours)",
    y = "Model",
    color = "Battery")

ggp2_clev_dots <- ggplot(data = walkman_clev_dots,
                mapping = aes(x = med_hours, 
                              y = fct_rev(model))) +
                geom_line(aes(group = model), 
                    linewidth = 0.75) + 
                geom_point(aes(color = battery), 
                    size = 2.25) 

(
  ggp2_clev_dots +
      labs_clev_dots
) +
  fmggp2::theme_walkman(base_size = 12) +
  bare_theme
```

[^amounts-def]: Counts or simple summary statistics of one or two columns in a dataset.

[^grp-vars]: Grouped bar graphs compare multiple variables across the same categories, with a cluster of bars for each category.

[^grp-axes]: The `x` axis labels the categories, and the `y` axis shows the measured value.

[^grp-legend]: Colors (or patterns) differentiate the subsets, and a legend identifies them.

[^statistic]: A summary statistic for each category, like the mean, median, or total.

[^median]: The median.

[^error-bars]: Error bars, which show variation or confidence intervals.

[^overlap]: Overlapping bar graphs.

[^alpha]: Partially transparent bars (set with `alpha`), so opaque bars don't hide the ones behind them.

[^matrix]: A matrix of cells, with categories on the `x` and `y` axes.

[^color-scale]: A color scale (legend).

[^grid]: Instead of the slices in a pie chart, waffle charts use squares or icons arranged in a grid.

[^percent]: Percentages or proportions of a total.

[^efficient]: Cleveland dot plots (named for William S. Cleveland) are often more efficient than traditional bar graphs.
